title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
State Farm's lawyers used an AI tool called Irys to prepare court filings in a lawsuit over a house fire and water damage, believing it would verify legal citations. The tool instead generated fake cases, nonexistent quotes, and fabricated legal holdings. Seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles. The lawyers discovered these errors and apologized to the court and plaintiff.

This was a failure to verify AI output before submitting it to a court. The tool was deployed in a high-stakes legal setting where accuracy is essential and where courts rely on citations to real cases. A simple check against actual case databases, either manual or automated, would have caught the fabrications before they reached the court.

Whether the lawyers' belief that Irys performed citation verification was justified by the tool's documentation or marketing is not established.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit have apologized for using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and fabricated legal holdings in their court filings. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire in her Carson home left it uninhabitable. During reconstruction, a storm caused water damage, and after delays in getting State Farm's approval for repairs, the work was never completed. Meni-Siliga and her husband subsequently depleted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure.

State Farm lawyer Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the errors and apologized to the court and plaintiff, explaining that a colleague used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare filings. The tool was mistakenly believed to perform citation verification. Another State Farm lawyer, Jacquelene Robinson, confirmed that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. The trial is scheduled for October, and the case highlights growing concerns about AI hallucinations in legal work, with a Paris-based database documenting 1,922 such cases worldwide.
